subject: Chemistry

mods.t: Atomic structure and the periodic table
Inorganic chemistry and the periodic table
Formulae, equations and amounts of substance

cards: CHEM.MASS_NUMBER
Define mass number.
The total number of **protons and neutrons** in the nucleus of an atom
CHEM.ATOMIC_NUMBER
Define atomic number.
The **number of protons** in the nucleus of an atom
CHEM.ISOTOPES
Define isotopes.
Atoms of the same element with the **same number of protons** and **different numbers** of **neutrons**
CHEM.AR
Define relative atomic mass.
The **weighted mean** mass of an atom of an element compared with **one twelfth** of the mass of an atom of **carbon-12**
CHEM.RIM
Define relative isotopic mass.
The **mass of an atom of an isotope** compared with **one twelfth** of the mass of an atom of **carbon-12**
CHEM.TOF_STAGES
Name the four stages of time-of-flight mass spectrometry.
**Ionisation**, **acceleration**, **ion drift** and **detection**
CHEM.ELECTROSPRAY
How does electrospray ionisation ionise a sample?
The sample is dissolved and sprayed from a fine needle at a **high voltage**, so each molecule **gains a proton** and becomes a 1+ ion
CHEM.ELECTRON_IMPACT
How does electron impact ionise a sample?
**High-energy electrons** from an electron gun **knock an electron off** each particle, forming a 1+ ion
CHEM.TOF_SEPARATION
How are ions separated in a time-of-flight mass spectrometer?
Every ion gets the **same kinetic energy**, so **lighter ions move faster** and reach the detector first
CHEM.MASS_SPECTRUM_AR
How is relative atomic mass found from a mass spectrum?
Multiply each isotope's m/z by its **relative abundance**, add these, and divide by the **total abundance**
CHEM.ORBITAL
What is an orbital?
A region around the nucleus that can hold up to **two electrons**, with **opposite spins**
CHEM.SUBSHELL_ORDER
In what order are the sub-shells filled up to 4p?
1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p: the **4s fills before the 3d**
CHEM.CR_CU
Why are chromium and copper exceptions to the filling order?
One 4s electron moves into the 3d sub-shell, giving the more stable half-full or full 3d: Cr is [Ar] **3d5 4s1** and Cu is [Ar] **3d10 4s1**
CHEM.IONS_4S
Which electrons does a transition metal lose first when it forms an ion?
The **4s** electrons, before any 3d electrons
CHEM.FIRST_IE
Define first ionisation energy.
The energy needed to remove one **electron** from each atom in **one mole** of **gaseous** atoms, forming one mole of gaseous **1+ ions**
CHEM.IE_ACROSS
Why does first ionisation energy generally rise across a period?
The **nuclear charge increases** while **shielding** stays similar, so the outer electron is **held more strongly**
CHEM.IE_DOWN
Why does first ionisation energy fall down a group?
The outer electron is **further from the nucleus** and **more shielded**, so it is held **less strongly**, despite the greater nuclear charge
CHEM.IE_AL
Why is the first ionisation energy of aluminium lower than that of magnesium?
Aluminium's outer electron is in a **3p** orbital, which is higher in energy and partly **shielded** by the **3s** electrons
CHEM.IE_S
Why is the first ionisation energy of sulfur lower than that of phosphorus?
In sulfur the electron is removed from a 3p orbital that holds a **pair**, and the **repulsion** between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove
CHEM.SUCCESSIVE_IE
What do successive ionisation energies show?
A **large jump** between two successive values shows that the next electron comes from a shell **closer to the nucleus**, which tells you the group
CHEM.MOLE
What is one mole of a substance?
The amount that contains the **Avogadro constant** of particles, **6.02 × 10²³**
CHEM.MOLAR_MASS
What is molar mass?
The **mass of one mole** of a substance, in g mol⁻¹
CHEM.RMM
Define relative molecular mass.
The **weighted mean** mass of a molecule compared with **one twelfth** of the mass of an atom of **carbon-12**
CHEM.MOLAR_GAS_VOLUME
What volume does one mole of any gas take up at room temperature and pressure?
About **24.0 dm³**, or 24 000 cm³
CHEM.EMPIRICAL
Define empirical formula.
The **simplest whole-number ratio** of atoms of each element in a compound
CHEM.MOLECULAR_FORMULA
Define molecular formula.
The **actual number** of atoms of each element in a molecule
CHEM.WATER_OF_CRYSTALLISATION
What is water of crystallisation?
Water molecules that are part of the **structure of a crystal**; a salt that has it is **hydrated**, one without it is **anhydrous**
CHEM.ATOM_ECONOMY
How is atom economy calculated?
Molar mass of the **desired product** ÷ total molar mass of **all the reactants** × 100
CHEM.PERCENT_YIELD
How is percentage yield calculated?
**Actual** amount of product ÷ **theoretical** amount × 100
CHEM.STANDARD_SOLUTION
What is a standard solution?
A solution whose **concentration is known accurately**
CHEM.CONCENTRATION
How is concentration in mol dm⁻³ calculated?
Amount in **moles** ÷ **volume in dm³**
CHEM.CONCORDANT
What are concordant titres?
Titres that agree within **0.10 cm³** of each other
CHEM.STATE_SYMBOLS
What do the four state symbols stand for?
(s) **solid**, (l) **liquid**, (g) **gas** and (aq) **aqueous** solution
CHEM.ION_FORMULAE
Give the formulae of the nitrate, sulfate, carbonate and ammonium ions.
**NO₃⁻**, **SO₄²⁻**, **CO₃²⁻** and **NH₄⁺**
CHEM.ACID
What is a Brønsted-Lowry acid?
A **proton donor**
CHEM.BASE
What is a Brønsted-Lowry base?
A **proton acceptor**
CHEM.ALKALI
What is an alkali?
A base that **dissolves in water**, releasing **hydroxide ions**
CHEM.STRONG_ACID
What is a strong acid?
An acid that **fully dissociates** in water
CHEM.WEAK_ACID
What is a weak acid?
An acid that only **partially dissociates** in water
CHEM.NEUTRALISATION
Give the ionic equation for neutralisation.
H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → **H₂O**(l)
CHEM.OXIDATION
Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons.
Oxidation is the **loss of electrons**; reduction is the **gain of electrons**
CHEM.OXIDISING_AGENT
What is an oxidising agent?
A species that **accepts** **electrons**, and is itself reduced
CHEM.REDUCING_AGENT
What is a reducing agent?
A species that **donates** **electrons**, and is itself oxidised
CHEM.OXIDATION_NUMBERS
State the oxidation number rules for an element, oxygen and hydrogen.
An uncombined element is **0**; oxygen is usually **−2** (−1 in peroxides); hydrogen is usually **+1** (−1 in metal hydrides)
CHEM.HALF_EQUATIONS
How are two half-equations combined into a redox equation?
Multiply them so the **electrons lost equal the electrons gained**, then add them and **cancel** the electrons
CHEM.DISPROPORTIONATION
Define disproportionation.
A redox reaction in which the **same element** is both **oxidised and reduced**
CHEM.IONIC_BOND
What is ionic bonding?
The strong **electrostatic attraction** between **oppositely charged ions**
CHEM.COVALENT_BOND
What is a covalent bond?
The strong electrostatic attraction between a **shared pair of electrons** and the **nuclei** of the bonded atoms
CHEM.DATIVE
What is a dative covalent bond?
A covalent bond in which **both electrons** of the shared pair come from the **same atom**
CHEM.METALLIC_BOND
What is metallic bonding?
The strong electrostatic attraction between **positive metal ions** and **delocalised electrons**
CHEM.ELECTRONEGATIVITY
Define electronegativity.
The power of an atom to **attract** the **pair of electrons** in a **covalent bond**
CHEM.POLAR_BOND
When is a covalent bond polar?
When the two atoms have **different electronegativities**, so the bonding pair is shared **unequally**
CHEM.NONPOLAR_MOLECULE
Why can a molecule with polar bonds be non-polar overall?
The molecule is **symmetrical**, so the bond dipoles **cancel**
CHEM.LONDON_FORCES
What causes induced dipole-dipole (London) forces?
An uneven spread of electrons makes an **instantaneous dipole**, which **induces a dipole** in a neighbouring molecule, and the two attract
CHEM.LONDON_SIZE
Why do London forces get stronger as molecules get bigger?
**More electrons** give **larger** instantaneous and induced dipoles, so the attractions between molecules are stronger
CHEM.HYDROGEN_BOND
What is needed for hydrogen bonding between molecules?
A hydrogen atom bonded to **nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine**, attracted to a **lone pair** on a nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine atom of another molecule
CHEM.ICE
Why is ice less dense than water?
**Hydrogen bonds** hold the molecules in an **open lattice**, further apart than in the liquid
CHEM.VSEPR
What decides the shape of a molecule?
The electron pairs around the central atom **repel** each other and spread **as far apart as possible**, and **lone pairs repel more** than bonding pairs
CHEM.TETRAHEDRAL
Give the bond angles in a tetrahedral, a pyramidal and a bent molecule.
**109.5°** in a tetrahedral molecule such as CH₄, **107°** in a pyramidal one such as NH₃, and **104.5°** in a bent one such as H₂O
CHEM.LINEAR_OCTAHEDRAL
Give the shape and bond angle for two and for six bonding pairs.
Two bonding pairs: **linear**, **180°**; six bonding pairs: **octahedral**, **90°**
CHEM.TRIGONAL_PLANAR
What shape and bond angle has a molecule with three bonding pairs and no lone pairs?
**Trigonal planar**, with bond angles of **120°**
CHEM.DIAMOND
Why does diamond have a very high melting point?
It is a **giant covalent** lattice, so many **strong covalent bonds** must be broken
CHEM.GRAPHITE
Why does graphite conduct electricity?
Each carbon atom bonds to only **three** others, leaving one **delocalised electron** per atom that can move between the layers
CHEM.IONIC_CONDUCTION
When do ionic compounds conduct electricity?
When **molten** or **dissolved**, because the **ions** are then **free to move**
CHEM.SIMPLE_MOLECULAR
Why do simple molecular substances have low melting points?
Only the **weak forces between molecules** need to be overcome, **not the covalent bonds**
CHEM.PERIODICITY
What is periodicity?
A **repeating trend** in properties across each period
CHEM.BLOCKS
What decides which block an element is in?
The **sub-shell** that holds its **highest-energy electron**
CHEM.ATOMIC_RADIUS
Why does atomic radius decrease across Period 3?
The **nuclear charge increases** while **shielding** stays similar, so the outer electrons are **pulled closer**
CHEM.METAL_MELTING
Why do melting points rise from sodium to aluminium?
The metal ions have a **greater charge** and there are **more delocalised electrons**, so the metallic bonding is **stronger**
CHEM.SILICON
Why does silicon have the highest melting point in Period 3?
It has a **giant covalent** structure, with many **strong covalent bonds** to break
CHEM.G2_REACTIVITY
Why does reactivity increase down Group 2?
The atoms get larger and **more shielded**, so the two outer electrons are **lost more easily**
CHEM.G2_WATER
What forms when a Group 2 metal reacts with water?
A metal **hydroxide** and **hydrogen**; magnesium reacts with steam to form magnesium oxide instead
CHEM.G2_SOLUBILITY
How do the solubilities of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates change down the group?
The **hydroxides become more soluble**; the **sulfates become less soluble**
CHEM.G2_USES
Give a use of calcium hydroxide and of magnesium hydroxide.
Calcium hydroxide neutralises **acidic soil**; magnesium hydroxide is an **antacid** for indigestion
CHEM.BARIUM_MEAL
Why is barium sulfate safe to use in a barium meal?
It is **insoluble**, so the toxic barium ions are **not absorbed** into the blood
CHEM.THERMAL_STABILITY
Why are Group 2 carbonates more thermally stable further down the group?
The cations are larger with the same charge, so they have a lower **charge density** and **polarise** the carbonate ion less
CHEM.FLAME_TESTS
What flame colours do lithium, sodium, potassium and calcium ions give?
Lithium **red**, sodium **yellow-orange**, potassium **lilac**, calcium **brick-red**
CHEM.FLAME_COLOUR_WHY
Why do metal ions give colours in a flame?
Heat **excites electrons** to higher energy levels, and as they **fall back** they **emit light** of particular frequencies
CHEM.HALOGEN_BOILING
Why do the boiling points of the halogens rise down the group?
The molecules have **more electrons**, so the **London forces** between them are stronger
CHEM.HALOGEN_OXIDISING
Why do the halogens become weaker oxidising agents down the group?
The atoms are larger and **more shielded**, so they **gain an electron less readily**
CHEM.DISPLACEMENT
What does a halogen displacement reaction show?
A **more reactive halogen** oxidises the **halide ions** of a less reactive one
CHEM.HALIDE_TEST
How are halide ions identified with silver nitrate?
Add dilute nitric acid then **silver nitrate**: chloride gives a **white** precipitate, bromide a **cream** one and iodide a **yellow** one
CHEM.HALIDE_AMMONIA
How does ammonia confirm which silver halide formed?
Silver chloride dissolves in **dilute ammonia**, silver bromide only in **concentrated ammonia**, and silver iodide **does not dissolve**
CHEM.NITRIC_FIRST
Why is nitric acid added before silver nitrate in the halide test?
To remove **carbonate** or hydroxide ions, which would also form a **precipitate**
CHEM.HALIDE_SULFURIC
Why do bromide and iodide react differently from chloride with concentrated sulfuric acid?
They are **stronger reducing agents**, so they **reduce the sulfuric acid**: to SO₂ with bromide, and on to S and H₂S with iodide
CHEM.CHLORINE_WATER
Why is chlorine added to drinking water although it is toxic?
It **kills bacteria**, and the benefit to health **outweighs** the small risk from its toxicity
CHEM.BLEACH
How is bleach made from chlorine?
Chlorine reacts with **cold**, dilute **sodium hydroxide** to give **sodium chlorate(I)**, sodium chloride and water
CHEM.CARBONATE_TEST
How is the carbonate ion tested for?
Add a **dilute acid**; fizzing of a gas that turns **limewater milky** shows carbonate
CHEM.SULFATE_TEST
How is the sulfate ion tested for?
Add acidified **barium** chloride or barium nitrate; a **white precipitate** of barium sulfate shows sulfate
CHEM.AMMONIUM_TEST
How is the ammonium ion tested for?
Warm it with **sodium hydroxide**; **ammonia** gas is given off, which turns **damp red litmus paper blue**
CHEM.TEST_ORDER
In what order should anion tests be done, and why?
**Carbonate**, then **sulfate**, then **halide**, so that no ion added in an earlier test gives a **false positive**
CHEM.ENTHALPY_CHANGE
What is an enthalpy change?
The **heat energy** transferred in a reaction at **constant pressure**
CHEM.STANDARD_CONDITIONS
What are standard conditions?
**100 kPa**, a stated temperature (usually **298 K**), and solutions at **1 mol dm⁻³**
CHEM.EXO_ENDO
What do exothermic and endothermic mean for the sign of ΔH?
An exothermic reaction releases heat to the surroundings, so ΔH is **negative**; an endothermic reaction takes heat in, so ΔH is **positive**
CHEM.FORMATION
Define standard enthalpy of formation.
The enthalpy change when **one mole** of a compound forms **from its elements** in their **standard states**, under **standard conditions**
CHEM.COMBUSTION
Define standard enthalpy of combustion.
The enthalpy change when **one mole** of a substance burns **completely** in **oxygen** under **standard conditions**
CHEM.NEUTRALISATION_ENTHALPY
Define standard enthalpy change of neutralisation.
The enthalpy change when an acid and a base react to form **one mole of water** under **standard conditions**
CHEM.CALORIMETRY
Give the equation for the heat energy measured in calorimetry.
The equation **q = mcΔT**, where m is the **mass** of the water or solution being heated
CHEM.CALORIMETRY_ERRORS
Why is a measured enthalpy of combustion usually less exothermic than the data book value?
**Heat is lost** to the surroundings, combustion is **incomplete**, and the conditions are **not standard**
CHEM.HESS
State Hess's law.
The enthalpy change of a reaction is **independent of the route** taken
CHEM.MEAN_BOND_ENTHALPY
What is mean bond enthalpy?
The enthalpy needed to **break one mole** of a given bond in **gaseous** molecules, **averaged over many** different compounds
CHEM.BOND_ENTHALPY_ERROR
Why do enthalpy changes worked out from mean bond enthalpies differ from data book values?
Mean values are **averages** over many compounds, **not the exact** bonds in this reaction
CHEM.ACTIVATION
Define activation energy.
The **minimum energy** **colliding** particles need for a **reaction** to happen
CHEM.COLLISION_THEORY
What must happen for particles to react, by collision theory?
They must **collide** with the **correct orientation** and with at least the **activation energy**
CHEM.MAXWELL_BOLTZMANN
What does the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution show?
The spread of **kinetic energies** of the molecules in a gas; the curve starts at the **origin** and the **area under** it is the total number of molecules
CHEM.TEMPERATURE_RATE
Why does a small rise in temperature greatly increase the rate?
Many more molecules have energy at or above the **activation energy**, and collisions are **more frequent**
CHEM.CONCENTRATION_RATE
Why does a higher concentration or pressure increase the rate?
There are more particles in the **same volume**, so collisions are **more frequent**
CHEM.CATALYST
What is a catalyst?
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing an **alternative route** with a **lower activation energy**, and is **not used up**
CHEM.HOMOGENEOUS
How do homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts differ?
A homogeneous catalyst is in the **same phase** as the reactants; a heterogeneous catalyst is in a **different phase**
CHEM.MEASURE_RATE
Name two ways to follow the rate of a reaction that gives off a gas.
Measure the volume of gas with a **gas syringe**, or the **loss of mass** on a balance, over time
CHEM.DYNAMIC_EQUILIBRIUM
What is dynamic equilibrium?
In a **closed system**, the forward and reverse reactions happen at the **same rate**, so the **concentrations stay constant**
CHEM.LE_CHATELIER
State le Chatelier's principle.
If a system at equilibrium is changed, the **position of equilibrium** shifts to **oppose the change**
CHEM.CATALYST_EQUILIBRIUM
How does a catalyst affect an equilibrium?
It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions **equally**, so equilibrium is reached **sooner** but its **position does not change**
CHEM.COMPROMISE
Why is a compromise temperature used for an exothermic industrial equilibrium such as the Haber process?
A low temperature gives a **higher equilibrium yield** but too slow a **rate**, so a moderate temperature balances yield and rate
CHEM.KC_MEANING
What does the size of Kc tell you?
A **large** Kc means the equilibrium lies to the right, towards the **products**; a small one means it lies to the **left**
CHEM.KC_CHANGE
What changes the value of Kc?
**Only temperature**; concentration, pressure and catalysts do not change it
CHEM.K_EXOTHERMIC
What happens to K for an exothermic reaction when the temperature rises?
**K decreases**, because the equilibrium shifts in the **endothermic direction**, towards the reactants
CHEM.PARTIAL_PRESSURE
What is a partial pressure?
The pressure one gas in a mixture would exert on its own: its **mole fraction** × the **total pressure**
CHEM.MOLE_FRACTION
What is a mole fraction?
The **moles of one gas** divided by the **total moles** of gas in the mixture
CHEM.KP_SOLIDS
Which species appear in a Kp expression?
**Only the gases**; **solids and liquids** are left out
CHEM.RATE_EQUATION
What is a rate equation?
Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where m and n are the **orders** with respect to A and B, found only by **experiment**
CHEM.ORDER
What is the order with respect to a reactant?
The **power** to which its **concentration** is raised in the **rate equation**
CHEM.OVERALL_ORDER
What is the overall order of a reaction?
The **sum of the orders** with respect to each reactant
CHEM.RATE_CONSTANT_T
How does the rate constant change when temperature rises?
The **rate constant increases**, so the rate increases
CHEM.HALF_LIFE
What is special about the half-life of a first-order reaction?
It is **constant**, whatever the starting concentration
CHEM.ZERO_ORDER
What does a concentration-time graph look like for a zero-order reactant?
A **straight line** with a negative gradient, because the rate **does not change** with concentration
CHEM.RATE_CONC_GRAPHS
What do rate-concentration graphs look like for zero, first and second order?
Zero order is a **horizontal line**, first order a **straight line through the origin**, and second order an **upward curve**
CHEM.RDS
What is the rate-determining step?
The **slowest step** in a reaction mechanism; the species in the rate equation take part in it or in steps before it
CHEM.CONJUGATE
What is a conjugate acid-base pair?
Two species that **differ by one proton**
CHEM.PH
Define pH.
The **negative logarithm** to base 10 of the **hydrogen ion concentration**: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]
CHEM.KW
What is the ionic product of water, Kw?
Kw = **[H⁺][OH⁻]**, which is 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at **298 K**
CHEM.KA
Write the expression for Ka of a weak acid HA.
CHEM.WEAK_ACID_APPROX
What two approximations are used to find the pH of a weak acid?
**[H⁺] = [A⁻]**, because the water's own dissociation is ignored, and the equilibrium [HA] equals the **starting concentration**, because so little dissociates
CHEM.PKA
What is pKa?
The value **−log₁₀ Ka**; the smaller the pKa, the **stronger** the acid
CHEM.BUFFER
What is a buffer solution?
A solution that **resists changes in pH** when **small amounts** of acid or base are added
CHEM.ACIDIC_BUFFER
How does an ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate buffer work?
Added acid is removed by the large reservoir of **ethanoate ions**, which form **ethanoic acid**; added alkali is removed by ethanoic acid reacting with the **OH⁻** ions
CHEM.BLOOD_BUFFER
What buffer system controls the pH of blood?
The **carbonic acid** and **hydrogencarbonate** ion system
CHEM.INDICATOR
How is an indicator chosen for a titration?
Its **colour change** must happen within the steep, **vertical part** of the titration curve
CHEM.HALF_NEUTRALISATION
What is special about the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration?
There [HA] = [A⁻], so **pH = pKa**
CHEM.EQUIVALENCE
What is the equivalence point of a titration?
The point where the acid and base have reacted **exactly** in the ratio of the equation
CHEM.ATOMISATION
Define standard enthalpy of atomisation.
The enthalpy change when **one mole of gaseous atoms** forms from the element in its **standard state**
CHEM.ELECTRON_AFFINITY
Define first electron affinity.
The enthalpy change when each atom in **one mole** of **gaseous** atoms **gains one electron** to form one mole of gaseous **1− ions**
CHEM.SECOND_EA
Why is a second electron affinity endothermic?
The electron is added to a **negative ion**, which **repels** it, so energy must be put in
CHEM.HYDRATION_ENTHALPY
Define enthalpy change of hydration.
The enthalpy change when one mole of **gaseous ions** dissolves in water to form one mole of **aqueous ions**
CHEM.SOLUTION_ENTHALPY
Define enthalpy change of solution.
The enthalpy change when **one mole** of an ionic solid **dissolves** in enough water that its ions are fully separated
CHEM.LATTICE_SIZE
What makes a lattice enthalpy more exothermic?
**Smaller ions** with **larger charges**, which attract each other more strongly
CHEM.COVALENT_CHARACTER
Why can a lattice enthalpy from a Born-Haber cycle differ from the theoretical value?
The theoretical value assumes **perfectly ionic** bonding, but a small, highly charged cation **polarises** the anion, giving some **covalent character**
CHEM.ENTROPY
What is entropy?
A measure of the **dispersal** of energy, or the **disorder**, in a system
CHEM.ENTROPY_STATES
Which state of matter has the highest entropy?
**Gases**, then liquids, then solids
CHEM.GIBBS
When is a reaction feasible?
When **ΔG = ΔH − TΔS** is zero or **negative**
CHEM.FEASIBLE_TEMPERATURE
Above what temperature does a reaction with positive ΔH and positive ΔS become feasible?
Above T = **ΔH ÷ ΔS**, when TΔS outweighs ΔH
CHEM.FEASIBLE_NOT_FAST
Why might a feasible reaction not happen at all?
Its **activation energy** may be so high that the **rate** is negligible
CHEM.ELECTRODE_POTENTIAL
Define standard electrode potential.
The **emf** of a half-cell measured against the **standard hydrogen electrode**, under **standard conditions**
CHEM.HYDROGEN_ELECTRODE
Describe the standard hydrogen electrode.
Hydrogen gas at **100 kPa** bubbled over a **platinum** electrode in 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺ ions at **298 K**; its potential is defined as **0.00 V**
CHEM.PLATINUM
Why is platinum used as the electrode in some half-cells?
It is **inert** and **conducts**, so it gives a surface for electron transfer when neither species is a solid metal
CHEM.SALT_BRIDGE
What does a salt bridge do?
It **completes the circuit** by letting **ions** move between the half-cells, without the solutions mixing
CHEM.CELL_EMF
How is a standard cell emf calculated?
E(cell) = the **more positive** electrode potential **minus the less positive** one
CHEM.FEASIBILITY_E
How do electrode potentials predict whether a redox reaction happens?
The half-cell with the **more positive** E° is **reduced** and the one with the more negative E° is oxidised; the reaction is feasible if E(cell) is **positive**
CHEM.FEASIBILITY_LIMITS
Why might a reaction predicted by E° values not happen?
It may be **too slow** because its activation energy is high, or **non-standard conditions** may change the potentials
CHEM.FUEL_CELL
What is a fuel cell?
A cell that makes a voltage from a **fuel**, such as hydrogen, reacting with **oxygen**, with a **continuous supply** of both
CHEM.RECHARGEABLE
How is a rechargeable cell recharged?
An external current **reverses** the cell reactions, re-forming the reactants
CHEM.MANGANATE_TITRATION
Why is no indicator needed in a manganate(VII) titration?
The manganate(VII) ions are **purple** and are reduced to almost **colourless** Mn²⁺ ions, so the end point is the first **permanent pink**
CHEM.IODINE_THIOSULFATE
What indicator is used in an iodine-thiosulfate titration, and when is it added?
**Starch**, added near the end point when the solution is **pale yellow**; the end point is when the **blue-black** colour disappears
CHEM.PERIOD3_OXIDES
How do the Period 3 oxides behave in water?
Sodium and magnesium oxides are **basic**, aluminium oxide is **amphoteric** and insoluble, and the oxides of the non-metals are **acidic**
CHEM.AMPHOTERIC
What does amphoteric mean?
Able to react as **both an acid and a base**, as aluminium oxide and aluminium hydroxide do
CHEM.TRANSITION_ELEMENT
What is a transition element?
A **d-block** element that forms at least one **stable ion** with an **incomplete d sub-shell**
CHEM.SC_ZN
Why are scandium and zinc not transition elements?
Sc³⁺ has an **empty** 3d sub-shell and Zn²⁺ a **full** one, so neither forms an ion with an **incomplete d sub-shell**
CHEM.TRANSITION_PROPERTIES
Name the characteristic properties of transition elements.
**Variable oxidation states**, **coloured** ions, **catalytic** activity and the formation of **complex ions**
CHEM.LIGAND
What is a ligand?
A molecule or ion that donates a **lone pair** of electrons to a metal ion, forming a **coordinate bond**
CHEM.COMPLEX_ION
What is a complex ion?
A **central metal ion** surrounded by **ligands** joined to it by **coordinate bonds**
CHEM.COORDINATION_NUMBER
What is the coordination number of a complex?
The **number of coordinate bonds** to the central metal ion
CHEM.BIDENTATE
What is a bidentate ligand?
A ligand that forms **two coordinate bonds** to the metal ion, such as ethane-1,2-diamine or the ethanedioate ion
CHEM.CHELATE_EFFECT
Why does a multidentate ligand readily replace monodentate ones?
The **number of particles** in solution increases, so the **entropy increases** and ΔG is negative
CHEM.COMPLEX_SHAPES
What shapes do complexes with six, four and two ligands have?
Six: **octahedral**; four: **tetrahedral**, or **square planar** as in cisplatin; two: **linear**, as in [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺
CHEM.CIS_TRANS_COMPLEX
Which isomerism can octahedral and square planar complexes show?
**Cis-trans** isomerism, and octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands can also show **optical** isomerism
CHEM.CISPLATIN
How does cisplatin act as an anticancer drug?
It **binds to DNA** in cancer cells, stopping the DNA **replicating**, so the cells **cannot divide**
CHEM.COMPLEX_COLOUR
Why are transition metal complexes coloured?
Ligands **split the d orbitals**; electrons **absorb** light of one frequency to jump to the higher level, and the **complementary colour** is seen
CHEM.COLOUR_CHANGE
What changes the colour of a transition metal complex?
A change of **oxidation state**, **ligand** or **coordination number**, which changes the energy gap ΔE
CHEM.COLORIMETRY
How is a colorimeter used to find the concentration of a coloured ion?
Measure the **absorbance** of **standard solutions** of known concentration, plot a **calibration curve**, and read the unknown's concentration from its absorbance
CHEM.VANADIUM
What colours are vanadium's +5, +4, +3 and +2 oxidation states?
**Yellow** (VO₂⁺), **blue** (VO²⁺), **green** (V³⁺) and **violet** (V²⁺)
CHEM.TOLLENS
What is Tollens' reagent, and what does it show?
[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺; warmed with an **aldehyde** it gives a **silver mirror**, while a **ketone** gives no change
CHEM.AUTOCATALYSIS
What is autocatalysis?
A reaction **catalysed by one of its own products**, such as Mn²⁺ in the reaction of manganate(VII) with ethanedioate
CHEM.CATALYST_POISONING
What is catalyst poisoning?
**Impurities** bond to the surface of a heterogeneous catalyst, blocking its **active sites**
CHEM.VARIABLE_OX_CATALYST
Why are transition metals good catalysts?
They have **variable oxidation states**, so they can take part in electron transfer and provide an alternative route with a **lower activation energy**
CHEM.CU_AMMONIA
What happens when ammonia solution is added to aqueous copper(II) ions, a little then in excess?
A **pale blue precipitate** of copper(II) hydroxide forms, then dissolves in excess to give a **deep blue solution** of [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺
CHEM.CU_CHLORIDE
What happens when concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to aqueous copper(II) ions?
The six water ligands are replaced by **four chloride** ligands, giving a **yellow** solution of **tetrahedral** [CuCl₄]²⁻
CHEM.HYDROXIDE_PRECIPITATES
What colours are the hydroxide precipitates of Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺?
Cu²⁺ gives **blue**, Fe²⁺ **green** and Fe³⁺ **orange-brown**
CHEM.CARBON_MONOXIDE
Why is carbon monoxide toxic?
It replaces oxygen as a **ligand** on the iron in **haemoglobin** and binds **more strongly**, so less oxygen is carried
CHEM.AQUA_ACIDITY
Why are solutions of M³⁺ aqua ions more acidic than those of M²⁺?
The 3+ ion has a **higher charge density**, so it **polarises** its water ligands more and they **release H⁺** ions more readily
CHEM.METAL_TESTS_OCR
How do you tell Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ apart with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
Fe²⁺ gives a **green precipitate** that turns brown in air; Fe³⁺ gives an **orange-brown precipitate**
CHEM.HOMOLOGOUS_SERIES
What is a homologous series?
A family of compounds with the **same functional group** and **general formula**, each member differing from the next by **CH₂**
CHEM.FUNCTIONAL_GROUP
What is a functional group?
The group of atoms responsible for a compound's **characteristic reactions**
CHEM.FORMULA_TYPES
What do displayed and skeletal formulae show?
A displayed formula shows **every atom and every bond**; a skeletal formula shows the carbon chain as **lines**, with only the functional groups drawn
CHEM.STRUCTURAL_ISOMERS
What are structural isomers?
Compounds with the **same molecular formula** but a **different structural formula**
CHEM.STEREOISOMERS
What are stereoisomers?
Compounds with the **same structural formula** but a different **arrangement of atoms in space**
CHEM.EZ_CONDITIONS
Why do some alkenes have E/Z isomers?
Rotation about the C=C double bond is **restricted**, and each carbon of the double bond has **two different groups** attached
CHEM.EZ_RULES
How do you decide whether an isomer is E or Z?
Rank the two groups on each carbon by **atomic number** (the CIP rules); in Z the higher-priority groups are on the **same side**, in E on **opposite sides**
CHEM.FISSION
What is the difference between homolytic and heterolytic fission?
In homolytic fission each atom keeps **one electron**, forming two **radicals**; in heterolytic fission one atom takes **both electrons**, forming **ions**
CHEM.RADICAL
What is a radical?
A species with an **unpaired electron**
CHEM.CURLY_ARROW
What does a curly arrow show?
The **movement of a pair of electrons**, from a bond or a lone pair towards an atom
CHEM.NUCLEOPHILE
What is a nucleophile?
An **electron pair donor**
CHEM.ELECTROPHILE
What is an electrophile?
An **electron pair acceptor**
CHEM.SATURATED
What is a saturated hydrocarbon?
A compound of **hydrogen and carbon only**, with **single bonds only**
CHEM.FRACTIONAL_DISTILLATION
How does fractional distillation separate crude oil?
The oil is **vaporised** and the vapours rise up a column that is **cooler at the top**; fractions condense at different heights by their **boiling points**
CHEM.CRACKING
What is cracking, and why is it done?
Breaking **long-chain alkanes** into **shorter** alkanes and **alkenes**, which are more useful and in **higher demand**
CHEM.CRACKING_TYPES
How do thermal and catalytic cracking differ?

Thermal cracking uses a **high temperature and pressure** and gives a high proportion of alkenes; catalytic cracking uses a **zeolite** catalyst at a lower temperature and gives branched alkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons for fuels
CHEM.REFORMING
What is reforming?
Turning straight-chain alkanes into **branched** alkanes and **cyclic** hydrocarbons, which burn more efficiently in engines
CHEM.BRANCHING
Why do branched alkanes boil lower than their straight-chain isomers?
Branches stop the molecules packing closely, so there is less **surface contact** and there are **weaker London forces** between them
CHEM.INCOMPLETE_COMBUSTION
Why is incomplete combustion dangerous?
It forms **carbon monoxide**, a **toxic** gas, and soot
CHEM.NOX
How do nitrogen oxides form in an engine, and how are they removed?
Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the **high temperature** in the engine; a **catalytic converter** turns them back into nitrogen
CHEM.FLUE_GAS
How is sulfur dioxide removed from power station waste gases?
By reacting it with **calcium oxide** or **calcium carbonate**
CHEM.RADICAL_STAGES
Name the three stages of free-radical substitution.
**Initiation**, **propagation** and **termination**
CHEM.INITIATION
What happens in the initiation step when methane is chlorinated?
**UV light** breaks the Cl–Cl bond by **homolytic fission**, forming two **chlorine radicals**
CHEM.RADICAL_MIXTURE
Why does free-radical substitution give a poor yield of one product?
**Further substitution** and different termination steps give a **mixture of products**
CHEM.OZONE_DEPLETION
How do CFCs destroy ozone?
UV light breaks C–Cl bonds, releasing **chlorine radicals**, which **catalyse** the breakdown of **ozone** into oxygen
CHEM.HYDROLYSIS_RATE
Why do iodoalkanes hydrolyse fastest of the haloalkanes?
The C–I bond has the **lowest bond enthalpy**, so it breaks most easily, even though it is the **least polar**
CHEM.SUBSTITUTION_ELIMINATION
What conditions make hydroxide ions substitute rather than eliminate with a haloalkane?
Warm **aqueous** hydroxide gives **substitution**, making an alcohol; hot hydroxide in **ethanol** gives **elimination**, making an alkene
CHEM.EXCESS_AMMONIA
Why is excess ammonia used to make a primary amine from a haloalkane?
With **excess** ammonia, the amine formed is less likely to **react further** to give secondary and tertiary amines
CHEM.PI_BOND
What is a π bond?
The **sideways overlap** of adjacent **p orbitals**, above and below the plane of the bonded carbon atoms
CHEM.SIGMA_BOND
What is a σ bond?
The direct, **head-on overlap** of orbitals between two bonded atoms
CHEM.ALKENE_REACTIVITY
Why are alkenes more reactive than alkanes?
The C=C double bond is a region of **high electron density**, and its **π bond** has a low bond enthalpy
CHEM.CARBOCATION_STABILITY
What decides the major product when HBr adds to an unsymmetrical alkene?
The **more stable carbocation** intermediate: **tertiary** carbocations are more stable than secondary, which are more stable than primary
CHEM.BROMINE_WATER
How do you test for a C=C double bond?
Shake with **bromine water**; it decolourises from **orange to colourless**
CHEM.ADDITION_POLYMERISATION
What is addition polymerisation?
The joining of many **alkene monomers**, as their **double bonds** open, into one long chain with **no other product**
CHEM.POLYMER_WASTE
Name three ways of dealing with waste polymers.
**Recycling**, **burning** for energy, and using them as a **feedstock** for cracking and new plastics
CHEM.POLYALKENE_INERT
Why are poly(alkenes) not biodegradable?
Their C–C and C–H bonds are strong and **non-polar**, so they are **unreactive**
CHEM.ALCOHOL_CLASSES
How are alcohols classified as primary, secondary or tertiary?
By how many carbons are bonded to the carbon carrying the OH: one for **primary**, two for **secondary**, three for **tertiary**
CHEM.ALCOHOL_OXIDATION
What do primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols give with acidified dichromate?
Primary alcohols give **aldehydes**, then **carboxylic acids** under reflux; secondary give **ketones**; tertiary are **not oxidised**; the orange dichromate turns **green**
CHEM.DISTIL_REFLUX
Why distil to make an aldehyde but reflux to make a carboxylic acid?
Distilling **removes the aldehyde** as it forms, so it is not **oxidised further**; refluxing keeps it in the flask until it is **fully oxidised**
CHEM.DEHYDRATION
How is an alcohol dehydrated?
Heat it with a **concentrated** **acid** catalyst such as phosphoric or sulfuric acid, which **eliminates water** and forms an **alkene**
CHEM.FERMENTATION
State the conditions for making ethanol by fermentation.
**Yeast**, glucose in water, about 35 °C, and **anaerobic** conditions
CHEM.ETHENE_HYDRATION
How is ethanol made industrially from ethene?
Ethene reacts with **steam** at about 300 °C and 60 atm over a **phosphoric acid catalyst**
CHEM.CARBON_NEUTRAL
Why is bioethanol not truly carbon neutral?
Energy from **fossil fuels** is used to grow, harvest, transport and distil it
CHEM.REFLUX
Why is a mixture heated under reflux?
Vapours **condense** and **return** to the flask, so it can be heated for a long time without losing volatile reactants or products
CHEM.PURIFY_LIQUID
How is an organic liquid purified after a reaction?
Wash it in a **separating funnel**, dry it with an **anhydrous** salt such as magnesium sulfate, then **redistil** it, collecting the fraction at its **boiling point**
CHEM.IR_ABSORPTION
What makes a bond absorb infrared radiation?
The bond absorbs infrared at the frequencies that make it **vibrate** more, by stretching or bending
CHEM.FINGERPRINT_REGION
What is the fingerprint region of an infrared spectrum?
The region **below about 1500** cm⁻¹, whose pattern is **unique** to a compound and can be matched against a database
CHEM.GREENHOUSE_IR
Why are carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour greenhouse gases?
Their bonds **absorb** the **infrared** radiation given out by the Earth's surface
CHEM.BREATHALYSER
How is infrared used in a breathalyser?
The **absorption** by the C–H bonds of **ethanol** is measured, and its strength shows the amount of alcohol in the breath
CHEM.MOLECULAR_ION
What does the molecular ion peak show?
The M⁺ peak at the **highest m/z** value, ignoring the small M+1 peak, gives the **relative molecular mass**
CHEM.FRAGMENTATION
What happens when a molecular ion fragments?
It breaks into a **positive ion**, which is detected, and a **radical**, which is not
CHEM.HIGH_RESOLUTION_MS
What does high-resolution mass spectrometry allow?
M/z values to several **decimal places**, which tell apart compounds with the same whole-number mass and so give the **molecular formula**
CHEM.CHIRAL_CENTRE
What is a chiral centre?
A carbon atom bonded to **four different groups**
CHEM.ENANTIOMERS
What are enantiomers, and how are they told apart?
**Non-superimposable mirror images**, which rotate **plane-polarised light** in **opposite directions**
CHEM.RACEMIC
What is a racemic mixture, and why is it optically inactive?
An **equal mixture** of two enantiomers; their rotations of plane-polarised light **cancel** out
CHEM.SN1_SN2
How can optical activity show whether a substitution is SN1 or SN2?

SN2 attack from the side opposite the leaving group inverts the configuration, giving one optically active product; SN1 goes through a **planar carbocation**, attacked from **either side**, giving a **racemic mixture**
CHEM.HCN_ADDITION
Why does adding HCN to an unsymmetrical ketone give a racemic mixture?
The carbonyl group is **planar**, so the cyanide ion is equally likely to attack from **either side**
CHEM.NABH4
What does NaBH₄ do to aldehydes and ketones?
It reduces aldehydes to **primary alcohols** and ketones to **secondary alcohols**
CHEM.DNPH
How is a carbonyl group detected?
Add **2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine** (Brady's reagent); an **orange precipitate** forms
CHEM.FEHLINGS
How does Fehling's solution tell an aldehyde from a ketone?
Warmed with an aldehyde it turns from **blue** to a **brick-red precipitate**; a **ketone** gives no change
CHEM.IODOFORM
What does the iodoform test detect?
A **CH₃CO** group, or an alcohol that is oxidised to one: warming with iodine and alkali gives a **pale yellow precipitate**
CHEM.ESTERIFICATION
How is an ester made from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid?
Warm them with a **concentrated sulfuric acid** catalyst
CHEM.ESTER_HYDROLYSIS
How do acid and alkaline hydrolysis of an ester differ?
Acid hydrolysis is **reversible** and gives the carboxylic acid; alkaline hydrolysis goes to **completion** and gives the **carboxylate** salt
CHEM.SOAP
What do fats and oils give when they are hydrolysed with sodium hydroxide?
**Glycerol** and the sodium salts of fatty acids, which are **soaps**
CHEM.BIODIESEL
How is biodiesel made?
Vegetable oils react with **methanol**, using a catalyst, to give **methyl esters** of fatty acids
CHEM.ACYL_CHLORIDES
Why are acyl chlorides used rather than carboxylic acids to make esters?
They react quickly and **irreversibly** at room temperature, giving a **better yield**
CHEM.ADDITION_ELIMINATION
Name the mechanism of acyl chlorides with nucleophiles.
**Nucleophilic addition-elimination**
CHEM.CARBOXYLIC_TEST
How do you show that a compound is a carboxylic acid?
Add sodium **carbonate** or sodium hydrogencarbonate; it fizzes, giving **carbon dioxide**
CHEM.BENZENE_EVIDENCE
What evidence shows benzene does not have Kekulé's structure?
Its enthalpy of hydrogenation is **less exothermic than expected** for three C=C bonds, its C–C bonds are all the **same length**, and it **resists addition** reactions
CHEM.BENZENE_BONDING
Describe the bonding in benzene.
A **planar** ring of six carbons, each with one **p orbital**; these overlap to form a ring of **delocalised** π electrons above and below the plane
CHEM.NITRATION
How is benzene nitrated?
With **concentrated nitric** and **sulfuric** acids at up to 55 °C; the sulfuric acid helps form the **nitronium ion**, NO₂⁺, which is the electrophile
CHEM.FRIEDEL_CRAFTS
What is the catalyst in Friedel-Crafts acylation, and what does it do?
**Aluminium chloride**, a halogen carrier, which reacts with the acyl chloride to form the **acylium ion** electrophile
CHEM.PHENOL_BROMINE
Why does phenol react with bromine water more readily than benzene?
A **lone pair** on the oxygen is partly **delocalised** into the ring, raising its **electron density**, so bromine is polarised more easily
CHEM.DIRECTING_GROUPS
Which positions do OH and NH₂ groups direct substitution to, and which does NO₂?
OH and NH₂ direct to the **2- and 4-** positions; NO₂ directs to the **3-** position
CHEM.AMINES_BASES
Why are amines bases?
The **lone pair** on the nitrogen atom can **accept a proton**
CHEM.BASE_STRENGTH
Why is ethylamine a stronger base than ammonia, and phenylamine a weaker one?
The alkyl group pushes electron density onto the nitrogen, making its lone pair **more available**; in phenylamine the lone pair is **delocalised** into the ring, making it **less available**
CHEM.NITRILE_TO_AMINE
How can a primary amine be made from a nitrile?
Reduce it with **LiAlH₄**, or with hydrogen over a **nickel** catalyst
CHEM.PHENYLAMINE_PREP
How is phenylamine made from nitrobenzene?
Reduce it with **tin** and **concentrated hydrochloric acid**, then add **sodium hydroxide**
CHEM.AMINES_NUCLEOPHILES
Why can amines act as nucleophiles?
The nitrogen has a **lone pair** it can **donate** to an electron-deficient carbon
CHEM.ZWITTERION
What is a zwitterion?
An ion with both a **positive and a negative charge**, as an amino acid is at its **isoelectric point**
CHEM.PROTEIN_HYDROLYSIS
How are proteins hydrolysed in the laboratory?
Boil with 6 mol dm⁻³ **hydrochloric acid** for several hours, breaking the **peptide** links
CHEM.ENZYME_STEREOSPECIFIC
Why can two enantiomers of a drug have different effects?
The active site of an enzyme or a receptor is **stereospecific**, so only **one enantiomer** fits
CHEM.DNA_STRANDS
What holds the two strands of DNA together?
**Hydrogen bonds** between complementary bases: **adenine with thymine**, and **cytosine with guanine**
CHEM.CONDENSATION_POLYMER
What is condensation polymerisation?
Monomers with **two functional groups** join, losing a **small molecule** such as water or HCl at each link
CHEM.CONDENSATION_BIODEGRADE
Why can polyesters and polyamides be broken down, unlike poly(alkenes)?
Their ester and amide links are **polar**, so they can be **hydrolysed**
CHEM.GRIGNARD
What is a Grignard reagent, and why is it useful?
RMgBr, made from a halogenoalkane and **magnesium** in **dry ether**; it makes new **carbon-carbon bonds** with carbonyl compounds
CHEM.CYANIDE_CHAIN
Why is the cyanide ion useful in synthesis?
It **adds one carbon atom** to the chain, making a **nitrile** that can be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine
CHEM.SYNTHESIS_ROUTE
What should a good synthetic route have?
As **few steps** as possible, a **high yield** at each step, and a high **atom economy**
CHEM.RECRYSTALLISATION
How is an impure organic solid purified by recrystallisation?
Dissolve it in the **minimum volume of hot solvent**, filter while hot, **cool** to crystallise, filter under **reduced pressure**, wash with cold solvent and dry
CHEM.MELTING_POINT
How does a melting point show purity?
A pure solid melts **sharply** at its known melting point; impurities **lower** the melting point and **widen** the range
CHEM.TMS
Why is TMS used in NMR spectroscopy?
It gives a **single** strong peak, which is the **reference** at δ = 0 ppm, and it is **inert** and volatile
CHEM.DEUTERATED_SOLVENT
Why are deuterated solvents used in proton NMR?
They contain **no ordinary hydrogen** atoms, so they give **no peak** of their own
CHEM.N_PLUS_ONE
What is the n + 1 rule in proton NMR?
A peak for protons with n protons on the **adjacent carbon** is split into **n + 1** peaks
CHEM.PEAK_AREA
What does the relative area under each peak in proton NMR show?
The **relative number** of hydrogen atoms in each **environment**
CHEM.D2O
How can an OH or NH proton be identified in proton NMR?
Add **D₂O**: the OH or NH peak **disappears**, because the proton is swapped for deuterium
CHEM.C13_NMR
What does the number of peaks in a carbon-13 NMR spectrum show?
The number of **different carbon environments**
CHEM.COMBINED_TECHNIQUES
What does each technique tell you when you deduce a structure?
Mass spectrometry gives the **Mr**, infrared gives the **functional groups**, and NMR gives the carbon and hydrogen **environments**
CHEM.RF_VALUE
How is an Rf value calculated?
**Distance moved by the spot** ÷ distance moved by the **solvent front**
CHEM.CHROMATOGRAPHY
How does chromatography separate substances?
Each substance is shared differently between the **stationary phase** and the **mobile phase**, so they move at **different rates**
CHEM.RETENTION_TIME
What is retention time in gas chromatography?
The time a component takes to pass through the **column** to the **detector**
CHEM.FUNCTIONAL_TESTS
Give the test and positive result for a primary or secondary alcohol, or an aldehyde.
Warm with **acidified potassium dichromate**; it turns from **orange to green**
CHEM.VALID_PLAN
What makes a plan valid?
It tests only the effect of the **independent variable**, with every other variable **controlled**
CHEM.BURETTE_UNCERTAINTY
What is the uncertainty of a titre from a burette?
±**0.05 cm³** for each reading, so ±**0.10 cm³** for a titre worked out from two readings
CHEM.PRECISE_RESULTS
What are precise results?
Repeated results that are **close to each other**
CHEM.PERCENTAGE_UNCERTAINTY
How is percentage uncertainty calculated?
**Uncertainty** ÷ **measured value** × 100
CHEM.HAZARD_RISK
What is the difference between a hazard and a risk?
A hazard is anything that **could cause harm**; a risk is the **chance** of that harm happening
CHEM.KC_EXPRESSION
How is a Kc expression written?
The concentrations of the **products**, each raised to the **power** of its number in the balanced equation, multiplied together and divided by those of the **reactants** in the same way
CHEM.WEAK_NEUTRALISATION
Why is the enthalpy of neutralisation of a weak acid less exothermic than that of a strong acid?
Some of the energy released is used to finish **dissociating** the weak acid as it reacts, so **less energy** is given out overall
CHEM.GIBBS_K
How is ΔG linked to the equilibrium constant K?
ΔG = −RT ln K, so a **negative** ΔG means K is **greater than 1** and the equilibrium lies towards the **products**
CHEM.POLYESTER
What two kinds of monomer make a polyester?
A **diol** and a **dicarboxylic acid**, which join by **ester** links with water lost at each link
